title: Implement disaster recovery processes: decision comparison 1
teachingQuestion: Who declares, restores, validates, accepts, and transitions DR service?
caption: Compare meaning, decision conditions, and failures. These concise distinctions are paired with the worked examples in the teaching unit.

nodes.label: Disaster Recovery Process
nodes.definition: The accountable process for restoring mission-critical technology and its dependencies after a disaster, within approved business recovery objectives.
nodes.decision: Activate based on declared impact, recovery priorities, available strategy, authority, and safety conditions.
nodes.failureExample: Treating DR as only backup restoration misses people, communications, dependencies, validation, and business acceptance.
nodes.detail: The accountable process for restoring mission-critical technology and its dependencies after a disaster, within approved business recovery objectives.

nodes.label: Emergency Response
nodes.definition: Immediate actions that protect life, stabilize the event, preserve essential evidence, and enable a safe handoff to assessment and recovery.
nodes.decision: Prioritize life safety and incident stabilization before recovery acceleration; coordinate with authorized responders.
nodes.failureExample: Starting technical restoration while hazards or active compromise remain can harm people or destroy evidence.
nodes.detail: Immediate actions that protect life, stabilize the event, preserve essential evidence, and enable a safe handoff to assessment and recovery.

nodes.label: Damage Assessment
nodes.definition: The rapid assessment that determines affected scope, criticality, safety constraints, and feasible recovery options.
nodes.decision: Use current evidence to choose whether to recover in place, use an alternate capability, or escalate.
nodes.failureExample: Selecting a site or restore path before assessing dependencies can make the chosen plan impossible to execute.
nodes.detail: The rapid assessment that determines affected scope, criticality, safety constraints, and feasible recovery options.

nodes.label: Recovery Team
nodes.definition: The assigned technical and business participants who execute recovery tasks and communicate status under designated authority.
nodes.decision: Select members and alternates for the services, facilities, suppliers, skills, and shifts actually in scope.
nodes.failureExample: A team with no business owner or dependency expertise may restore infrastructure without restoring the required service.
nodes.detail: The assigned technical and business participants who execute recovery tasks and communicate status under designated authority.

nodes.label: Alternate Site
nodes.definition: A prearranged recovery location or capability selected to meet service objectives while avoiding the primary event’s correlated risks.
nodes.decision: Choose based on recovery-time/data objectives, capacity, geographic and utility separation, security controls, and test evidence.
nodes.failureExample: A nearby or untested site can share the same disaster impact or fail to support required capacity and security.
nodes.detail: A prearranged recovery location or capability selected to meet service objectives while avoiding the primary event’s correlated risks.

nodes.label: Backup Storage
nodes.definition: Protected recovery copies and their storage service, managed for recoverability, integrity, access control, retention, and required recovery point.
nodes.decision: Select based on recovery-point objective, restoration time, geographic/administrative separation, immutability or protection needs, and proven restore process.
nodes.failureExample: A copy is not a recovery capability if it is inaccessible, corrupted, too old, compromised, or cannot be restored in time.
nodes.detail: Protected recovery copies and their storage service, managed for recoverability, integrity, access control, retention, and required recovery point.

nodes.label: Return To Normal
nodes.definition: A deliberate exit from recovery mode after validated service, reconciled data, accepted residual risk, communications, and documented closure.
nodes.decision: Transition when stable normal operations and all required acceptance evidence are available.
nodes.failureExample: Switching back solely because systems are up can reintroduce unresolved defects or abandon temporary safeguards.
nodes.detail: A deliberate exit from recovery mode after validated service, reconciled data, accepted residual risk, communications, and documented closure.

nodes.label: Recovery Communications
nodes.definition: Managed communications that provide accurate decisions, status, constraints, and instructions to each relevant audience throughout recovery.
nodes.decision: Use alternate channels, message ownership, approved facts, notification thresholds, and recorded decisions.
nodes.failureExample: Uncoordinated updates can cause unsafe actions, duplicated work, misinformation, or regulatory/customer harm.
nodes.detail: Managed communications that provide accurate decisions, status, constraints, and instructions to each relevant audience throughout recovery.
